newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ABARE sees aluminium restart up to one mln/t.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ABARE sees aluminium restart up to one mln/t.

text.p: Unused world aluminium smelting capacity of up to one million tonnes could be restarted over the next two years, the Australian Bureau of Agricutural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.

It is unlikely the entire one million tonnes would be restarted although enough capacity could return to limit any near-term rise in aluminium prices and, over the medium term, even depress prices, ABARE said in a paper for delivery at its annual commodities conference later on Tuesday.
"This is despite projected sustained growth in global demand," ABARE said.

The capacity was idled as part of a now-expired memorandum of understanding between major aluminium-producing nations to cut production and shore up prices hurt by swollen inventories. However higher utilisation, coupled with expansions of existing smelters and start-up of new ones, threaten to outpace forecast annual growth, estimated at between two percent and 4.5 percent this year, ABARE said.

"With nearly a million tonnes of capacity still idle and a similar amount under construction, smelter output increases could easily overwhelm expected demand growth," Jim Southwood, president of consultants Commodity Metals Management Co said in a paper scheduled for delivery at the conference on Thursday. "With exisiting idle capacity in the hands of a few major producers, we can assume it will only be activated when market prices are more attractive," Southwood said.
New capacity under construction, though, will be completed regardless of the aluminium price, he added.

Current world smelter capacity utilisation is about 93 percent, Rod Kinkead-Weekes, managing director of Comalco Minerals and Alumina, an arm of Comalco Ltd, said in another paper to be delivered at the conference.

ABARE also said uncertainty surrounds future production of aluminium from Russia. "Russia's exports of primary aluminium to the West ... could fall sharply in 1997 if producers decide to sell more (aluminium) to domestic semi-fabricators, particularly if domestic demand for aluminium improves significantly in the context of stronger economic growth," ABARE said.
